lessons.title: Fake Bank Fraud Alert
lessons.body: The scammer wants your debit card verification number (the 3-digit code on back) and personal details to make fake purchases or steal your money.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, this is Sarah from First National Bank security team. We detected a suspicious charge of $2,450 on your debit card at an electronics store in Texas just 20 minutes ago. Did you make this purchase?" "To protect your account, I need to verify your identity right now. Can you tell me the numbers on the back of your debit card and your full address? If we don't act fast, someone could drain your entire account."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer wants your card verification number (the 3-digit code on back) and personal details to make fake purchases or steal your money. They create urgency by claiming a recent "suspicious charge" to pressure you into sharing sensitive info immediately.
lessons.consequences: If they get your card details, they can buy thousands of dollars in goods online or withdraw cash from ATMs. Your bank account could be emptied in hours, and recovering the money might take months or never happen.
danger_signs: Bank never asks for full card numbers over the phone.
They know details about a "recent charge" but pressure you to verify first.
Caller ID shows unfamiliar or blocked number.
They demand immediate action without giving you time to think.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up immediately. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or their official website (never use the number the caller gives you). Check your account online yourself to see if there's any real problem.

lessons.title: Medicare Reactivation Scam
lessons.body: The scammer pretends your Medicare benefits are about to expire to get your Medicare ID and Social Security number.
lessons.scammer_says: "Good morning, this is Mark from Medicare Services. Our records show your Medicare coverage expires next week because your card number didn't match our database. To reactivate it before you lose doctor visits and prescriptions, press 1 now and give us your Medicare number and Social Security number." "Don't worry, this takes just 2 minutes. Without this, you'll pay full price for all medical care."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer pretends your Medicare benefits are about to expire to get your Medicare ID and Social Security number. They use an automated recording or live caller to create panic about losing healthcare coverage.
lessons.consequences: With your Medicare and Social Security numbers, they can file fake medical claims, steal your identity for loans, or sell your info on the dark web. This could lead to ruined credit and years of identity theft problems.
danger_signs: Medicare never calls asking for your ID numbers.
They threaten to cancel benefits unless you act immediately.
Automated message asks you to "press 1" or provide personal info.
No official Medicare caller ID or reference number provided.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up or ignore the call. Contact Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) using a known good number to verify your coverage status. Your Medicare card never expires.

lessons.title: Technical Support Pop-up Scam
lessons.body: They trick you into a fake pop-up warning on your computer, then call pretending to be tech support.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, I'm David from SecureTech Support. Your computer just sent us a virus alert — it's infected with dangerous malware and freezing up. Don't turn it off! Let me connect remotely to fix it." "I see 1,247 viruses already. Give me permission to access your screen, and it'll cost just $199 to clean everything. Type this web address now: support-fix247.com."
lessons.the_trick: They trick you into a fake pop-up warning on your computer, then call pretending to be tech support. The goal is remote access to install more malware, steal files, or charge your card for fake "repairs."
lessons.consequences: Remote access lets them steal passwords, bank info, photos, and personal documents. They can lock your files for ransom or use your computer for illegal activities, making you responsible.
danger_signs: Pop-up claims "virus alert" and gives a phone number to call.
They ask for remote screen access or payment for "fixes."
Real companies like Microsoft never cold-call about viruses.
They mention specific scary numbers like "1,247 viruses."
lessons.safe_action: Close the pop-up without calling. Restart your computer in Safe Mode if worried. Run a free scan with antivirus software you trust, like Windows Defender. Never allow remote access to unknown callers.

lessons.title: Grandparent Emergency Scam
lessons.body: Scammer pretends to be your grandchild in trouble (arrested, accident, etc.) and asks for emergency money via wire transfer or gift cards.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma? It's me, Tommy. Don't tell Mom, but I got arrested in Mexico during a school trip. The police are holding me for $4,200 bail or they deport me tomorrow." "A lawyer named Robert will call you from 555-0123 to arrange wire transfer to my account. Please help, I'm scared."
lessons.the_trick: Scammer pretends to be your grandchild in trouble (arrested, accident, etc.) and asks for emergency money via wire transfer or gift cards. A second caller posing as "lawyer" or "police" adds pressure.
lessons.consequences: Wire transfers and gift cards can't be reversed. You lose thousands with no way to recover, and real grandchildren in trouble wouldn't ask for secrecy or untraceable payments.
danger_signs: Grandchild asks you to keep it secret from parents.
They sound wrong (young voice, accent, wrong name details).
Payment requested via wire transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency.
"Lawyer" or "police" refuse to give verifiable contact info.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up and call your real grandchild directly using a known phone number. Never send money without verifying in person or through trusted channels.

lessons.title: Utility Bill Disconnection Threat
lessons.body: Scammer claims unpaid utility bill and threatens immediate shutoff.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the electric company collections department. Your account #4783921 is overdue by $678. We will disconnect your power in 30 minutes unless you pay now with a prepaid debit card." "Go to the store and buy a $678 Green Dot card. Read me the numbers over the phone to avoid blackout."
lessons.the_trick: Scammer claims unpaid utility bill and threatens immediate shutoff. They demand instant payment via untraceable methods like prepaid cards or cryptocurrency to steal the money directly.
lessons.consequences: Once you give prepaid card numbers, the money vanishes instantly. No power gets disconnected because it was never your real utility company, and you can't get refunds from these payment methods.
danger_signs: Real utilities send written bills and give 7-30 days notice.
Demand for immediate payment in prepaid cards or other unusual payment method.
Refusal to send bill statement or accept check/credit card.
Unfamiliar phone number, not your utility's official line. (although sometimes they fake the name on Caller ID)
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Call your utility company using the number on your bill or website. Check your account balance online or in person. Real companies never demand instant prepaid card payments over the phone.

lessons.title: Delivery Package Scam
lessons.body: Fake text or email about a "missed delivery" tricks you into clicking links or calling.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi, this is Acme package delivery service. We attempted delivery of your item #TX847392 today but couldn't reach you. There's a $3.95 redelivery fee or the package returns to sender tomorrow." "Click this link or call 1-877-555-0198 to pay with your credit card. We need confirmation address too."
lessons.the_trick: Fake text or email about a "missed delivery" tricks you into clicking links or calling. They collect credit card numbers and addresses under pretense of small "redelivery fees."
lessons.consequences: The link installs malware or leads to phishing site that looks like a bank login, but steals your login information. Your card gets maxed out, and no package ever existed. Small fee request lowers suspicion.
danger_signs: Unsolicited message about package you didn't order.
Link to pay tiny fee ($1-5) or package "returned."
No legitimate tracking number provided upfront.
lessons.safe_action: Delete the message. Check your real delivery accounts (UPS, FedEx, USPS) using official apps or websites. Real companies leave notices at door or send from known email/text domains.

lessons.title: Fake Charity Disaster Appeal
lessons.body: Scammers call after real disasters pretending to be charity.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, I'm calling from Heartland Relief Fund for hurricane victims. We've set up emergency shelters but need $50 donations now. Can you please help with donation right now? A contribution from your credit card number is tax-deductible!" "Every dollar helps families right now. We'll mail receipt tomorrow."
lessons.the_trick: Scammers call after real disasters pretending to be charity. They collect credit card donations directly over phone, but the fake organization keeps all money for themselves.
lessons.consequences: Your card info gets used for repeated unauthorized charges. No aid reaches victims, no tax receipt arrives, and legitimate charities lose trust from the scam confusion.
danger_signs: Soliciting credit card donations cold-call style.
Vague charity name you've never heard of.
Pressure for immediate donation during disaster news.
No website or charity registration number provided.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Donate directly through known charities like Red Cross at redcross.org or local churches. Verify organizations at charitynavigator.org or guidestar.org before giving.

lessons.title: Fake Refund Overpayment
lessons.body: Claims you’re owed a refund from recent purchase to gain remote computer access.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Amazon refund department. We overcharged you $347.62 on your recent blender purchase. To issue refund, download this software and let us connect to your computer for 2 minutes." "Type teamviewer.com now and share the ID screen with me."
lessons.the_trick: Claims you’re owed a refund from recent purchase to gain remote computer access. While "processing refund," they install malware and steal banking passwords or personal data.
lessons.consequences: They reverse charges from your accounts instead of refunding. Malware logs keystrokes, stealing all passwords and enabling account takeovers across banks and email.
danger_signs: Unsolicited refund offer you didn't request.
Requires computer access or software download.
Real companies email refunds, not call for access.
They know purchase details to sound legitimate.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check your real account (Amazon, store website) for legitimate refund notices. Companies deposit refunds automatically or mail checks — they NEVER need remote access.

lessons.title: Mystery Shopper Job Scam
lessons.body: Fake job offer pays you to buy gift cards, then send card numbers/photos.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You have been approved for our mystery shopper position. Here's your first assignment: buy $950 in gift cards at the grocery store, take photos of receipts, then text us the card numbers for reimbursement." "You'll be reimbursed for the purchase PLUS earn $250 commission! Scratch off the back and read all numbers now."
lessons.the_trick: Fake job offer pays you to buy gift cards, then send card numbers/photos. They use the cards immediately while promising reimbursement that never arrives.
lessons.consequences: You lose hundreds spent on gift cards. Scammers drain cards instantly for cash or online purchases. Legitimate employers never ask employees to buy gift cards for payment.
danger_signs: A job that pays you to buy and send gift card numbers.
No formal application or interview process.
Email/text from free services like Gmail.
"Too good to be true" high pay for simple tasks.
lessons.safe_action: Delete offer. Real mystery shopper jobs come from established companies with websites, paychecks, and never require you to buy gift cards. Search company name + "scam" online first.

lessons.title: Romance Relationship Scam
lessons.body: Builds fake online romance over weeks/months, then invents emergencies (sick relative, travel trouble) needing urgent wire transfers.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi Linda, it's David from the dating site. I've enjoyed getting to know you over the past several weeks. I was planning to come visit, but my sister was in an accident and I gave her $1,800 for her surgery. Now I can't buy the $400 plane ticket to come see you." "I'll get the money back from her when she recovers, and I'll pay you back then, but to get the ticket at this price, can you wire the cost of the ticket to my account please? I can't wait to see you! ❤️"
lessons.the_trick: Builds fake online romance over weeks/months, then invents emergencies (sick relative, travel trouble) needing urgent wire transfers. Relationship provides emotional leverage for money requests.
lessons.consequences: Thousands sent over time via wire/gift cards, all unrecoverable. "Sweetheart" disappears after draining resources. Victims lose savings and suffer emotional betrayal.
danger_signs: Person avoids video calls or in-person meetings.
Always has emergencies needing wire transfers/gift cards.
Profile photos look professional or stolen online.
lessons.safe_action: Never send money to online contacts. Verify identity through video call or mutual friends. Report to FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov) and dating site. Real relationships develop without money requests.

lessons.title: IRS Tax Refund Scam
lessons.body: Pretends IRS owes you money to collect bank account details for direct deposit.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the Internal Revenue Service. You have an unclaimed refund of $1,872 waiting. Due to a filing error, we need your bank routing number and account number to direct deposit it today." "Press 1 to claim before funds return to Treasury, or call 1-888-555-0284."
lessons.the_trick: Pretends IRS owes you money to collect bank account details for direct deposit. Real IRS never calls unexpectedly about refunds or demands immediate bank info over phone.
lessons.consequences: Bank details let them drain accounts or create fake checks. IRS identity theft leads to tax problems, frozen refunds, and years repairing credit/government records.
danger_signs: IRS never calls demanding immediate bank info.
Threatens funds expire unless you act now.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. IRS sends refund checks by mail or direct deposits already on file. Check status at irs.gov using your own computer, never call numbers from unsolicited messages.

lessons.title: Home Repair Contractor Scam
lessons.body: Door-to-door "repair" claims urgent damage only they spotted.
lessons.scammer_says: "Ma'am, this is Mike's Roofing from down the street. I noticed you have some damaged shingles while driving by. Storm damage like this costs $8,000 to fix later, but I can do it today for $2,800 cash." "Pay half now, I'll start immediately before rain worsens it."
lessons.the_trick: Door-to-door "repair" claims urgent damage only they spotted. Takes large cash deposit then disappears or does shoddy work. Real roof issues don't require instant payment.
lessons.consequences: Lose thousands in deposits with no work done. Home damage worsens from neglect. Shoddy repairs fail quickly, costing double to fix properly later.
danger_signs: Unsolicited door knock claiming urgent home repair.
No written estimate or business license shown.
lessons.safe_action: Say no thanks. Get 3 written estimates from licensed contractors with reviews. Never pay more than 10% deposit. Check business license at state contractor board website.

lessons.title: Lottery Prize Scam
lessons.body: Claims you won lottery/sweepstakes you never entered.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You won $250,000 in the National Sweepstakes drawing. Entry #M7392847 selected you. To claim, send $498 processing fee via MoneyGram to our agent in Florida." "Winners must pay fees first. Call 1-800-555-0317."
lessons.the_trick: Claims you won lottery/sweepstakes you never entered. Demands "fees" (taxes, processing) via wire transfer before payout. Real winnings never require upfront payment.
lessons.consequences: Small fees escalate to thousands. No prize exists. Wire money gone forever. Credit ruined if they get enough personal info for identity theft.
danger_signs: Upfront fees required to claim prize.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up — real prizes never ask for money first. Verify at official lottery website. Report to FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Legitimate winnings contact you formally.

lessons.title: Government Grant Scam
lessons.body: Fake government grants for home repair/education.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You qualify for $5,000 government home improvement grant. No repayment needed. Send $250 processing fee to Federal Grant Processing Center via prepaid debit card." "Limited spots — pay today to lock in funds!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake government grants for home repair/education. Small "application fee" via prepaid cards unlocks "free money." Real grants never charge applicants.
lessons.consequences: Prepaid card money gone instantly. Escalating "fees" drain thousands. No grant exists. Personal info used for further scams or identity theft.
danger_signs: Payment via prepaid cards or wire transfer.
Unsolicited grant offers you never applied for.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Real grants through grants.gov require applications, never fees. Contact legitimate agencies directly. Report to ftc.gov/complaint.

lessons.title: Pharmacy Discount Scam
lessons.body: Unsolicited offer of prescription discounts asks for Medicare/health info.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is National Pharmacy Services. We can cut your prescriptions 85% with our discount card. Just give us your Medicare number and doctor's name to activate lifetime savings." "No cost to join — text back YES to enroll!"
lessons.the_trick: Unsolicited offer of prescription discounts asks for Medicare/health info. Fake "discount cards" steal insurance details for fraudulent claims and identity theft.
lessons.consequences: Medicare fraud billed to your number. Identity theft across healthcare system. Prescriptions denied when real claims flagged as suspicious. Years untangling medical records.
danger_signs: Text from short codes or unknown numbers.
"Free" card sounds too good to verify.
lessons.safe_action: Delete message. Use legitimate discount cards from GoodRx.com or your pharmacy chain. Never share Medicare number with discount services. Report to Medicare at 1-800-MEDICARE.

lessons.title: Apartment Rental Scam
lessons.body: Posts fake apartment listings with stolen photos.
lessons.scammer_says: "Perfect 2-bedroom apartment $1,200/month available immediately! Great photos online. Send $1,200 deposit via Zelle to hold before it's gone. Here's my number: 555-0199." "Moving out of state, need renter fast!"
lessons.the_trick: Posts fake apartment listings with stolen photos. Takes deposits via app transfers then disappears. Apartment doesn't exist or owner knows nothing about rental.
lessons.consequences: Lose deposit money instantly via app transfers. Homeless search restarts. Scammer repeats with next victim using same listing. Difficult recovery.
danger_signs: Landlord demands full deposit via app before seeing unit.
lessons.safe_action: Never send money without seeing apartment in person. Meet landlord/owner at property. Use written lease. Verify listing at apartmentratings.com. Cashier's check only after tour.

lessons.title: Car Warranty Scam
lessons.body: Robocall claims car warranty ending, pushes expensive "extended coverage." Uses vague vehicle details to sound legitimate.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Auto Protection Services. Your car warranty expires tomorrow. Extended coverage $1,899 locks in repairs for 5 years. Press 1 to speak Spanish or stay on line." "VIN ending 8472 confirmed. Give credit card for coverage."
lessons.the_trick: Robocall claims car warranty ending, pushes expensive "extended coverage." Uses vague vehicle details to sound legitimate. Real warranties don't cold-call for renewal.
lessons.consequences: Waste thousands on useless coverage. Card charged repeatedly. No service when repairs needed. Legitimate warranties through dealer/manufacturer only.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check real warranty through car dealer service department or manufacturer's website using VIN. Shop legitimate extended warranties through AAA or dealership only.

lessons.title: Social Security Scam
lessons.body: Threatens to suspend benefits unless you "verify" SSN over phone.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Social Security Administration fraud department. Suspicious activity on your SSN requires immediate suspension. Verify identity by giving full Social Security number and birthdate." "Failure to comply triggers law enforcement action."
lessons.the_trick: Threatens to suspend benefits unless you "verify" SSN over phone. Real Social Security never calls demanding immediate personal information verification.
lessons.consequences: SSN stolen enables identity theft, fake benefit claims, loans in your name. Benefits delayed while fraud investigated. Years cleaning up credit/government records.
danger_signs: Social Security demands SSN over phone.
Threats of arrest or benefit suspension.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Create mySocialSecurity account at ssa.gov to check status. Contact SSA at 1-800-772-1213 using known number. Report scam to oig.ssa.gov.

lessons.title: Investment Scam
lessons.body: Cold call pitches "guaranteed high returns" investments.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi Margaret, I'm Tom from Prosperity Investments. Our green energy fund returns 28% annually — double your neighbor's gains! Invest $10,000 minimum via wire transfer today." "Limited shares, first-time investors only."
lessons.the_trick: Cold call pitches "guaranteed high returns" investments. Takes money via wire transfer then disappears. Real investments carry risk, require registration.
lessons.consequences: Complete loss of investment principal. Wire transfers unrecoverable. Fake company vanishes. Retirement savings wiped out chasing unrealistic returns.
danger_signs: Wire transfer or crypto payment required.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Verify firm at sec.gov/EDGAR or finra.org/brokercheck. Work only with registered advisors. Investments promising guaranteed high returns = scams.

lessons.title: Jury Duty Arrest Scam
lessons.body: Claims missed jury duty warrant requires immediate "bail" payment via prepaid cards.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is County Sheriff's Office. You missed jury duty summons and a warrant has been issued for your arrest. Post $1,000 bail via prepaid cards or appear in 60 minutes at station." "Officer badge #8472. Don't hang up or the warrant activates."
lessons.the_trick: Claims missed jury duty warrant requires immediate "bail" payment via prepaid cards. Real police arrest in person, never demand payment over phone.
lessons.consequences: Lose bail money via untraceable prepaid cards. Escalating "fees" for court costs. Terrorized into compliance. No warrant ever existed.
danger_signs: Police demand prepaid cards or wire transfer.
Threat of immediate arrest over phone.
Refuse to verify through official channels.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Police arrest in person with uniform/warrant. Call local courthouse using 411 directory assistance number to verify status. Report to ftc.gov.

lessons.title: Magazine Prize Scam
lessons.body: Impersonates famous sweepstakes company claiming big win.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You won $5,000 from Publisher's Clearing House sweepstakes! Magazine subscriptions entered you automatically. Send $495 shipping/handling via MoneyGram to claim before 5PM today." "Big check and flowers delivered tomorrow!"
lessons.the_trick: Impersonates famous sweepstakes company claiming big win. Demands "shipping fees" via wire transfer. Real prizes never require payment to receive winnings.
lessons.consequences: "Fees" escalate from hundreds to thousands. No prize delivered. Wire money permanently lost. Victim waits endlessly for nonexistent delivery.
danger_signs: Prize you never entered requires payment first.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Real sweepstakes winners notified by mail, never pay to collect. Verify at pch.com directly. Report to ftc.gov/complaint.

lessons.title: Free Trial Scam
lessons.body: Small "shipping fee" enrolls you in expensive monthly autoship.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations!  You have been approved for a free 30-day trial of HealthMax Vitamins! Confirm your shipping address and credit card for $4.95 processing. Cancel anytime after first shipment." "After your free trial, monthly shipments will be $89.95 each, but you can cancel any time."
lessons.the_trick: Small "shipping fee" enrolls you in expensive monthly autoship. Hard-to-cancel subscriptions charge card repeatedly. Buried cancellation phone numbers.
lessons.consequences: Hundreds charged monthly for unwanted products. Cancellation battles fail. Credit card disputes denied for "recurring billing authorization."
danger_signs: "Free trial" asks for credit card upfront.
Small fee converts to expensive monthly charges.
lessons.safe_action: Never give card for "free trials." Use virtual credit cards or prepaid debit (with very limited funds on the card) for testing. Cancel in writing within 3 days. Dispute charges with bank.

lessons.title: Vaccine Certificate Scam
lessons.body: Fake government health verification demands Medicare info and fees.
lessons.scammer_says: "Health Department records show you need COVID vaccine verification for Medicare payments and doctor visits. Pay $39.95 processing fee for official digital certificate." "Email your Medicare number and card details to verify eligibility."
lessons.the_trick: Fake government health verification demands Medicare info and fees. No certificate issued, just stolen identity for medical fraud.
lessons.consequences: Medicare fraud destroys benefits. Identity theft across healthcare. Doctors refuse service when records flagged fraudulent.
danger_signs: Email demands Medicare info for certificates.
Payment required for government health docs.
lessons.safe_action: Delete message. Real vaccine records from healthcare provider only. Medicare status at 1-800-MEDICARE. Report to ftc.gov.

lessons.title: Storage Unit Scam
lessons.body: Fake "neighbor" sells nonexistent storage auction contents cheap.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi neighbor, it's Jim from across the street. My storage unit #247 at Mini-Store is auctioning tomorrow for unpaid rent. Contents worth $8,000 but you can claim for $950 cash today." "Furniture, tools, antiques — meet me at unit 3:30PM."
lessons.the_trick: Fake "neighbor" sells nonexistent storage auction contents cheap. Takes cash then disappears. Real auctions public with inspection.
lessons.consequences: Cash lost instantly. No storage unit exists. Scammer targets next neighborhood victim.
danger_signs: "Neighbor" you don't recognize selling storage contents.
Cash deal for valuable auction items.
No public auction listing or inspection.
lessons.safe_action: Call storage facility directly to verify auction. Attend public auctions only. Never buy sight-unseen valuables for cash from strangers.

lessons.title: Toll Violation Scam
lessons.body: Fake toll violations demand prepaid card payment.
lessons.scammer_says: "Toll Authority Collections — Vehicle #JHG-8472 has 6 unpaid tolls totaling $287 from your State Turnpike. Pay now via prepaid Visa card or vehicle registration suspended." "Read card numbers to agent or face $500 fine + towing."
lessons.the_trick: Fake toll violations demand prepaid card payment. Real toll agencies mail invoices, accept checks/credit cards.
lessons.consequences: Prepaid card drained instantly. No tolls existed. License clean but money gone forever.
danger_signs: Toll payment demands via prepaid cards.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check toll balance at your state's offical toll website. Real agencies mail bills first.

lessons.title: School Trip Emergency
lessons.body: Two-call scam: grandchild claims group travel emergency, teacher confirms.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma, it's Sarah from school trip to Washington DC. Bus broke down in Georgia, company demands $650 cash per student or whole group stranded overnight." "Teacher says send Western Union to bus company in Atlanta now."
lessons.the_trick: Two-call scam: grandchild claims group travel emergency, teacher confirms. Real school trips have emergency funds, insurance.
lessons.consequences: Western Union money gone instantly. No school trip problems exist. Grandchild safe at home.
danger_signs: Grandchild + teacher both call about group emergency.
School demands Western Union for trip issues.
lessons.safe_action: Call grandchild's home phone and school directly. Real emergencies go through the child's designated guardian first. Schools handle trip insurance.

lessons.title: Hotel Refund Scam
lessons.body: Fake hotel refund requires computer access.
lessons.scammer_says: "Sunset Inn front desk — your recent stay #847392 charged $247 extra. Refund processing requires remote access to verify payment info. Download TeamViewer now." "Share screen ID 928-374-192 for 2 minutes."
lessons.the_trick: Fake hotel refund requires computer access. Malware steals all passwords while "processing refund."
lessons.consequences: Banking passwords stolen. Accounts drained. No refund issued. Computer infected permanently.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check hotel account online directly. Real refunds by check/credit, never computer access.  NEVER give anyone that you don't know access with remote tools like TeamViewer.

lessons.title: Church Directory Scam
lessons.body: Fake church directory sales to members.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grace Community Church is publishing a directory. Your photo and family listing $125 full page, $89 half page. Provide credit card for professional photographer tomorrow." "All members participating — don't miss out!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake church directory sales to members. No directory produced. Church knows nothing about solicitation.
lessons.consequences: $89-125 charged, no directory. Card used for recurring charges.
danger_signs: No church announcement or bulletin notice.
lessons.safe_action: Call church office directly to verify. Real directories announced in services, payment to church treasurer.

lessons.title: Fence Contractor Scam
lessons.body: Door-to-door claims fence code violations.
lessons.scammer_says: "Ace Fence Company is canvassing neighborhood. Your fence is leaning dangerously — it's a code violation risk. $2,800 full replacement today, $1,400 half down cash." "County inspector coming next week — beat the fine!"
lessons.the_trick: Door-to-door claims fence code violations. Large cash deposit then poor work or disappearance. Real violations get written county notices.
lessons.consequences: $1,400 cash lost. Shoddy fence fails quickly. Code violation fine actually arrives later.
lessons.safe_action: Request written violation from county first. Get 3 licensed contractor bids. Never pay cash deposits.

lessons.title: Identity Protection Scam
lessons.body: Fake identity theft alerts demand full personal info access.
lessons.scammer_says: "IdentityGuard alert — your Social Security number appears on 7 dark web sites. $29.95/month monitoring removes it immediately. Provide SSN to enroll." "First month free if you start now!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake identity theft alerts demand full personal info access. Real monitoring services let you sign up without sharing your SSN over the phone.
lessons.consequences: Complete identity portfolio stolen. Multiple account takeovers. Credit destroyed across all bureaus.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check credit at annualcreditreport.com (free). Real services monitor externally, never access accounts. FTC identitytheft.gov for real help.

lessons.title: Tech Support Gift Card Scam
lessons.body: Fake tech support demands gift card purchases for "virus removal fees." They drain cards instantly while you watch.
lessons.scammer_says: "Microsoft technical support here. Your computer has 847 viruses detected. Don't panic — we can clear your computer.  Normally the fix is $249, but we partner with Google for a massive discount - you buy a $100 Google Play gift card from your local pharmacy or grocery store immediately. That gift card will qualify you for the discount." "Scratch off back, read 15-digit numbers to me now, and you can make your computer safe for the discounted price."
lessons.the_trick: Fake tech support demands gift card purchases for "virus removal fees." They drain cards instantly while you watch.
lessons.consequences: $100 gone in seconds. Gift cards untraceable. Computer never had viruses.
danger_signs: Tech support encourages gift card payments.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Run Windows Defender scan (free). Real tech support never requests gift cards. Report to ftc.gov.

lessons.title: Online Car Sale Scam
lessons.body: Fake car listing with stolen photos.
lessons.scammer_says: "2019 Toyota Camry 42K miles $12,500 FIRM — moving overseas, must sell fast! Email shipping deposit $1,200 via PayPal Friends & Family to hold car." "Broker arranges delivery to your driveway!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake car listing with stolen photos. Takes "shipping deposits" then disappears. Car never existed.
lessons.consequences: $1,200 lost instantly. Real car search restarts. Scammer posts same ad tomorrow.
lessons.safe_action: Always test drive in person. Pay dealer/bank check only. Verify VIN at carfax.com. Never wire money for unseen vehicles.

lessons.title: Funeral Prepayment Scam
lessons.body: Fake funeral preplanning steals life savings.
lessons.scammer_says: "Eternal Rest Planning Services — lock in funeral costs at today's rates! $4,800 prepaid trust fund guarantees mahogany casket, plot, service regardless of inflation." "Transfer to our funeral trust account today."
lessons.the_trick: Fake funeral preplanning steals life savings. No funeral services provided when needed. Real preplanning through licensed funeral homes only.
lessons.consequences: $4,800 gone when actually needed. No funeral services exist. Family pays double later.
lessons.safe_action: Plan directly with local licensed funeral homes. Use payable-on-death life insurance. Verify at funerals.org. Never prepay sight-unseen.

lessons.title: Solar Panel Rebate Scam
lessons.body: Fake government solar rebates demand processing fees.
lessons.scammer_says: "Federal Solar Energy Program — $8,500 rebate expires! Qualify now with $995 processing deposit to Energy Department trust. Panels installed for free after approval." "Government pays installation — you keep rebate!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake government solar rebates demand processing fees. No panels installed, no rebate issued.
lessons.consequences: $995 lost to nonexistent program. Real solar incentives through tax credits only. No panels, no savings.
lessons.safe_action: Government rebate programs change, so search official government sites, not depending on a stranger calling to provide the information. Government never demands deposits for rebates.

lessons.title: Grandchild Phone Scam
lessons.body: Two-scammer relay: "grandchild" claims lost phone, can't call parents.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma it's Alex — I lost my phone at the fair, I'm calling from the Apple store, which is why you don't recognize the number. I need a $300 iPhone deposit at Apple Store or I'm stranded till Dad returns Tuesday." "Put it on your card, I'll repay cash Friday ❤️"
lessons.the_trick: Two-scammer relay: "grandchild" claims lost phone, can't call parents. Real grandchild has phone, safe at home.
lessons.consequences: $300 charged to card. Grandchild never lost phone.
lessons.safe_action: Tell them you will call back.  Hang up, and call your grandchild's number. Then verify with their parents or guardian.

lessons.title: Airport Refund Scam
lessons.body: Fake airline refund steals all identity info.
lessons.scammer_says: "Delta Airlines refund department — cancelled flight #8472 entitles you to $478. Verify identity with credit card, SSN last 4, and mother's maiden name. Refund processes in 48 hours." "No ticket number needed."
lessons.the_trick: Fake airline refund steals all identity info. No flight cancellation occurred.
lessons.consequences: Complete identity theft portfolio. Credit cards maxed. No refund issued.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check airline account online directly. Real refunds auto-deposit to original payment method.

lessons.title: Driveway Sealing Scam
lessons.body: Door-to-door driveway "sealing" with watered-down asphalt.
lessons.scammer_says: "Neighborhood Seal Coating Special! A government oil embargo was announced, and seal coat prices triple next week. $1,400 cash for double driveway today." "Truck loaded, crews ready now!  Prices go up next week."
lessons.the_trick: Door-to-door driveway "sealing" with watered-down asphalt. Peels off in weeks (if they even coat anything at all). Large cash payment upfront.
lessons.consequences: $1,400 wasted. Real sealing requires proper prep, multiple coats. Driveway cracks worse.
danger_signs: Too cheap per square foot pricing.
lessons.safe_action: Get 3 written bids from licensed pavers. Avoid paying cash deposits.

lessons.title: Timeshare Cancellation Scam
lessons.body: Fake timeshare cancellation services take escrow fees but never resolve ownership.
lessons.scammer_says: "Timeshare Relief Team — we legally dissolve your maintenance fee burden! $4,500 escrow deposit guarantees cancellation within 90 days or full refund." "Deed transfer specialist standing by."
lessons.the_trick: Fake timeshare cancellation services take escrow fees but never resolve ownership. Timeshare remains, fees continue.
lessons.consequences: $4,500 lost. Still own timeshare, fees accrue. Foreclosure damages credit.
lessons.safe_action: Contact timeshare developer directly. Licensed real estate attorney only.  No legitimate upfront fees.

lessons.title: IRS Audit Scam
lessons.body: Fake IRS audit demands immediate bank access.
lessons.scammer_says: "IRS Audit Compliance — return #847392 flagged $8,247 underpayment. Pay penalty via our secure portal or face liens, levies. Provide bank info for direct debit." (You may receive a fake letter mailed separately.)
lessons.the_trick: Fake IRS audit demands immediate bank access. Real IRS sends certified mail first, never phone demands.
lessons.consequences: Bank account drained. Credit ruined. Real tax return fine if no audit notice received.
danger_signs: IRS demands bank info over phone.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Real IRS contacts by certified mail only. Check irs.gov account.

lessons.title: Extended Car Warranty Scam
lessons.body: Robocall panic warranty expiration.
lessons.scammer_says: "National Auto Warranty — your VIN #8472JG warranty expires midnight! $2,499 locks 100K miles bumper-to-bumper. All repairs nationwide, $0 deductible." "Enroll now or pay $5K transmission out-of-pocket!"
lessons.the_trick: Robocall panic warranty expiration. Useless contract denies all claims. Real warranties through manufacturer/dealer.
lessons.consequences: $2,499 wasted. Claims denied for "pre-existing." Repairs full price anyway.
lessons.safe_action: Check dealer service records. Real warranties mailed, not called. Manufacturer certified pre-owned only. Hang up on robocalls.
